case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Congress authorized cumulative punishments (and thus whether the Double Jeopardy Clause permits cumulative sentences) when the same firearm-related conduct yields convictions under both 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)(1)(A) and 18 U.S.C. § 924(j).
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. V (Double Jeopardy Clause); 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)(1)(A); 18 U.S.C. § 924(j).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Barrett argues that § 924(c)(1)(A) is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j) when both are based on the same firearm use during the same predicate crime, so cumulative sentencing on both counts for the same conduct is presumptively barred. Because Congress did not clearly indicate an intent to allow stacked punishments between § 924(c) and § 924(j)—unlike other places in § 924(c) where Congress expressly authorizes cumulative punishment—the presumption against multiple punishments is not rebutted, and one of the sentences (typically the § 924(c) sentence) must be vacated.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States (in this posture, supporting petitioner on the merits despite being the nominal respondent) agrees: § 924(c)(1)(A) is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j), triggering a presumption against cumulative punishment for the same conduct; that presumption can be rebutted only by a clear congressional statement, and no such clear statement exists here. In particular, § 924(c) contains explicit cumulative-punishment authorizations in some contexts but contains no language authorizing cumulation between § 924(c)(1)(A) and § 924(j), so the better reading is that Congress did not permit stacking these two punishments for the same firearm use and the same predicate crime.
key_precedents: Flowers v. Mississippi, 136 S. Ct. 2157 (2016) (Alito, J., dissenting) (GVR standard quotation)

John Roberts.reasoning: The Respondent’s best point is the “layering” intuition Justice Alito pressed—because § 924(j) applies only “in the course of a violation of subsection (c),” it can sound like Congress meant an added penalty. But as Justice Barrett and Justice Thomas emphasize, Missouri v. Hunter requires unmistakable authorization for cumulative punishments, and the statutory contrasts within § 924(c)—especially the “in addition to” clause keyed to the predicate offense and the consecutive-sentence command limited to sentences “under this subsection”—make § 924(j)’s silence on stacking (c) with (j) dispositive in the same-act, lesser-included posture. Lora, while not directly about multiplicity, reinforces that (j) operates on a distinct sentencing track, which undercuts any inference that Congress silently mandated a duplicative mandatory § 924(c) term on top of (j). I would keep the holding narrow to same-conduct cases where (c) is lesser-included in (j) and require vacatur of one sentence, leaving other scenarios for another day.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito’s structural point—that § 924(j) “in the course of a violation of subsection (c)” presupposes a completed (c) offense and thus authorizes an added (c) sentence—fails on the terms Missouri v. Hunter demands: unmistakable congressional authorization for the specific cumulative punishments at issue. As the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett explain, § 924(c)(1)(A)’s “in addition to” language is expressly keyed to the predicate crime’s punishment, and § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii)’s consecutive command is limited to sentences “under this subsection,” which undercuts any inference that Congress silently required (c)+(j) stacking. Because (j) incorporates all elements of (c) in the same-act scenario, Blockburger treats (c) as lesser-included; absent a clear statement, we do not presume Congress meant two punishments for the same offense. Lora, though addressing consecutiveness rather than multiplicity, reinforces that (j) is on a distinct sentencing track, making it even harder to read (j) as an automatic add-on rather than an alternative penalty when death results.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point is the “layering” intuition: § 924(j) applies only “in the course of a violation of subsection (c),” so one might think Congress contemplated an added (c) term. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett persuasively explain, Missouri v. Hunter demands unmistakable authorization for cumulative punishments in this same-act, lesser-included posture, and § 924(c)(1)(A)’s “in addition to” clause is textually keyed to the predicate offense—not to stacking another firearm count that already subsumes (c). Barrett’s contrast with § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii)’s limitation to sentences imposed “under this subsection,” together with Lora’s recognition that (j) follows a distinct sentencing track, undercuts any inference that Congress silently mandated (c)+(j) stacking. Given that residual ambiguity and the practical severity of duplicative mandatory terms, I would vacate one sentence rather than infer multiple punishments without clear statutory direction.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito’s structural point—that § 924(j) is “layered” because it applies only “in the course of a violation of subsection (c)”—still doesn’t answer the Missouri v. Hunter problem: we need an unmistakable statement that Congress authorized two punishments for the same firearm-use episode, not a plausible inference from statutory linkage. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, § 924(c)(1)(A)’s “in addition to” language is expressly about cumulating with the predicate crime, and Congress elsewhere in § 924(c) shows it knows how to mandate stacking expressly; that contrast makes the silence here meaningful. Lora (as Barrett notes) reinforces that (j) is on a distinct sentencing track, which fits reading (j) as the homicide penalty for the (c) conduct when death results—not an automatic extra mandatory add-on. Given the real-world severity of duplicative mandatory penalties and the lesser-included relationship in the same-conduct scenario (highlighted by Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch), any residual ambiguity should not be resolved to compound punishment without clear congressional direction.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point is Justice Alito’s “layering” argument: § 924(j) applies only “in the course of a violation of subsection (c),” which can sound like Congress assumed a (c) conviction plus an added homicide penalty. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett stress, Missouri v. Hunter asks for unmistakable authorization for cumulative punishments for the same conduct, and § 924(c)(1)(A)’s “in addition to” clause is textually keyed to the predicate offense—not to stacking (c) atop a separate provision that already incorporates (c). Barrett’s statutory-contrast point, reinforced by Lora’s recognition that (j) proceeds on a distinct sentencing track from “this subsection,” makes the absence of an express (c)+(j) stacking directive decisive under a pragmatic textualist approach aimed at coherent, administrable sentencing rules. I therefore continue to conclude that, in the same-act scenario where (c) is lesser-included in (j), one sentence must be vacated absent a clear congressional statement to the contrary.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The strongest opposing point is Justice Alito’s “layering” theory: because § 924(j) applies only “in the course of a violation of subsection (c),” Congress must have contemplated a (c) sentence plus an added homicide penalty. But Missouri v. Hunter demands unmistakable authorization for cumulative punishments, and as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett stress, § 924(c)(1)(A)’s “in addition to” clause is keyed to the predicate offense while § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii)’s consecutive-sentence rule is limited to sentences “under this subsection,” making § 924(j)’s silence on stacking dispositive under a textualist approach. Lora, as Justice Barrett notes, reinforces that § 924(j) proceeds on a distinct sentencing track, which undercuts reading (j) as an automatic add-on to (c) rather than an alternative penalty when death results. Given Blockburger’s lesser-included relationship on these facts, any residual ambiguity about cumulation is resolved against multiple punishments and, if needed, by lenity.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The respondent’s best point (pressed by Justice Alito) is the structural reading that § 924(j) operates “in the course of a violation of subsection (c),” suggesting Congress assumed a completed (c) offense and thus allowed an added penalty. But as the Chief Justice explains, Missouri v. Hunter requires unmistakable authorization for cumulative punishment for the same conduct, and § 924(c)(1)(A)’s “in addition to” is naturally keyed to the predicate crime, not to stacking a second firearm sentence on top of a (j) count that already incorporates the (c) elements in this same-act posture. Justice Barrett’s contrast argument—Congress repeatedly used explicit cumulation/consecutive language “under this subsection,” while (j) is silent—makes it especially hard, after Lora’s recognition that (j) follows a distinct sentencing track, to infer an extraordinary stacking regime from linkage alone. On an institutional, precedent-respecting approach, we should avoid expanding punitive duplication absent clear text, and require vacatur of one sentence where (c) is lesser-included in (j) on the same conduct.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The respondent’s best point is the “layering” inference Justice Alito identifies from § 924(j)’s phrase “in the course of a violation of subsection (c),” but that structural linkage is not the “unmistakable” authorization Missouri v. Hunter requires to impose cumulative punishment when Blockburger shows (c) is lesser-included in (j) on the same conduct. As the Chief Justice underscores, § 924(c)(1)(A)’s “in addition to” clause is textually keyed to the predicate offense, and § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii)’s consecutive-sentence command is expressly limited to sentences “under this subsection,” which cuts against silently stacking a (c) sentence atop a (j) sentence. Justice Thomas’s contrast argument is decisive: Congress repeatedly drafted explicit stacking and consecutiveness language in § 924(c), and § 924(j)’s silence—especially in light of Lora’s recognition that (j) proceeds on a distinct sentencing track—cannot do the work respondent assigns it. I therefore continue to read § 924(j) as the alternative penalty for the death-resulting firearm use in this same-act scenario, requiring vacatur of one sentence.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The strongest opposing point remains Justice Alito’s “layering” theory—that § 924(j) presupposes a completed § 924(c) and thus permits cumulative punishment—but structural intuition cannot substitute for the unmistakable authorization Missouri v. Hunter requires when the same act satisfies both provisions. As Justice Barrett and the Chief Justice emphasize, Congress knew how to write explicit cumulation and consecutiveness commands in § 924(c), and § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii)’s limitation to sentences imposed “under this subsection” makes § 924(j)’s silence on stacking with (c) highly consequential rather than permissive. Lora, though about consecutiveness, reinforces Barrett’s point that (j) operates on a distinct sentencing track, which undermines the claim that (j) silently mandates an additional (c) term. Given the severe practical consequences and the lesser-included relationship on these facts, I would not infer double punishment from ambiguity and would require vacatur of one sentence.

John Roberts.reasoning: When the same firearm use during the same predicate crime produces convictions under both § 924(c)(1)(A) and § 924(j), § 924(c) functions as a lesser-included offense of § 924(j), triggering the presumption against cumulative punishments absent a clear congressional statement. Under Missouri v. Hunter, the Double Jeopardy Clause permits cumulative sentences only where Congress has clearly authorized them; here, unlike other portions of § 924(c) that expressly mandate additional punishment, Congress did not speak clearly to stacking § 924(c) and § 924(j) for the same conduct. Reading the statutory structure narrowly to avoid unnecessary constitutional difficulty and to respect settled canons of construction, I would conclude Congress did not authorize cumulation and would require vacatur of one sentence. That disposition is limited and preserves institutional legitimacy by turning on congressional intent and statutory text rather than a broad constitutional rule.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Double Jeopardy Clause bars multiple punishments for the same offense unless Congress clearly authorizes cumulation, and the controlling inquiry is statutory text. Section 924(j) expressly applies “in the course of a violation of subsection (c)” and thus necessarily includes the elements of § 924(c)(1)(A) when both counts rest on the same firearm use during the same predicate crime, making § 924(c) a lesser-included offense in that circumstance. Unlike other provisions where Congress expressly mandates additional consecutive punishment (e.g., § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) and § 924(c)(5)), neither § 924(c)(1)(A) nor § 924(j) contains a clear statement authorizing stacked punishments between them, so under Missouri v. Hunter cumulative sentences are not permitted. Any remaining ambiguity about Congress’s authorization must be resolved against multiple punishments for the same offense.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Double Jeopardy question reduces to congressional intent: if Congress clearly authorized cumulative punishments, the Clause is not offended. Section 924(c)(1)(A) repeatedly mandates punishment “in addition to” the punishment for the predicate crime, and § 924(j) expressly applies when a defendant, “in the course of a violation of subsection (c),” causes death—linking (j) to a completed (c) violation rather than creating an alternative, mutually exclusive penalty. Under Missouri v. Hunter, that kind of explicit “in addition to” direction is sufficient to rebut any Blockburger-based presumption against multiple punishments, and reading (j) to silently displace (c) would undermine the practical, law-enforcement-facing design of § 924(c)’s mandatory additional punishment regime. Accordingly, I would uphold cumulative sentences for a single course of firearm use resulting in convictions under both provisions.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: When the same firearm use during the same predicate offense yields convictions under both 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)(1)(A) and § 924(j), § 924(c) functions as a lesser-included offense of § 924(j), triggering the presumption against cumulative punishments absent a clear congressional statement. Missouri v. Hunter makes clear that the Double Jeopardy Clause permits multiple punishments only when the legislature has clearly authorized them; here, Congress included explicit cumulation language elsewhere in § 924(c) but not for stacking § 924(c) with § 924(j), which cuts against inferring such authorization. In a system that must be fair and predictable—especially where mandatory consecutive firearm penalties can produce extreme sentences—ambiguity should not be resolved to impose additional punishment without clear statutory direction. Accordingly, one of the cumulative sentences must be vacated because Congress did not “specially authorize” punishment under both provisions for the same conduct.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: When the same firearm use during the same predicate offense supports convictions under both § 924(c)(1)(A) and § 924(j), § 924(c) functions as a lesser-included offense of § 924(j), triggering the presumption against cumulative punishments absent a clear congressional statement. Under Missouri v. Hunter, that presumption is rebutted only where the legislature makes its intent “crystal clear,” as with an express “in addition to” directive authorizing stacking for the same conduct. Congress used such explicit cumulative-punishment language in § 924(c) with respect to the predicate crime, but § 924(j) contains no comparable instruction authorizing an additional § 924(c) sentence on top of the § 924(j) penalty for the same firearm-related act. Reading the statute as a coherent, workable scheme, the better construction is that Congress authorized a single punishment for that conduct, so the Double Jeopardy Clause bars cumulation and one sentence must be vacated.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 924(j) by its terms applies only when a defendant causes death “in the course of a violation of subsection (c),” making a § 924(c)(1)(A) violation a necessary component and thus a lesser-included offense of § 924(j) for the same firearm use and predicate crime. Under Blockburger’s same-elements test, that triggers a presumption against cumulative punishments, and under Missouri v. Hunter that presumption may be overcome only by a clear congressional statement authorizing stacking. Here, § 924(c)(1)(A) expressly makes its punishment “in addition to” the predicate crime of violence or drug trafficking crime, but it does not say “in addition to” § 924(j), and § 924(j) contains no clear cumulation language either. Absent a clear statement, the Double Jeopardy Clause bars cumulative sentences for the same conduct, and any ambiguity is resolved against additional punishment under the rule of lenity.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under Missouri v. Hunter, the Double Jeopardy question turns on whether Congress clearly authorized cumulative punishment; absent that clear authorization, courts apply the usual presumption against multiple punishments for the same offense. Here, when § 924(j) is charged based on the same firearm use “in the course of” a § 924(c) predicate, § 924(c)(1)(A) functions as a lesser-included offense, and nothing in § 924(j) (or § 924(c)’s express cumulation provisions elsewhere) clearly indicates Congress intended stacked sentences for the same conduct. The consecutive-sentence mandate in § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) is best read to govern sentences “under this subsection,” not to silently require an additional consecutive punishment when the firearm homicide is punished under § 924(j). Respect for statutory text, traditional clear-statement principles in multiple-punishment cases, and practical workability counsel vacating the extra cumulative sentence.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Under Blockburger, § 924(c)(1)(A) is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j) when both convictions rest on the same firearm use during the same predicate crime, so cumulative punishment is presumptively barred absent a clear congressional statement. Missouri v. Hunter makes that presumption yield only where Congress has plainly authorized stacked punishments, but the text of § 924(j) contains no such authorization and, unlike other parts of § 924(c), does not expressly require cumulation with § 924(c). Congress’s demonstrated ability to specify cumulative punishments elsewhere in § 924(c) reinforces that its silence here cannot supply the “clear indication” needed to rebut the presumption against multiple punishments. Consistent with Lora v. United States’s recognition that § 924(j) takes a distinct sentencing approach from § 924(c), the better reading is that § 924(j) provides an alternative penalty for the same conduct, requiring one sentence (typically the § 924(c) sentence) to be vacated.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Because § 924(j) expressly incorporates “a violation of subsection (c),” 18 U.S.C. § 924(j), a § 924(c)(1)(A) conviction is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j) when both rest on the same firearm use during the same predicate crime, triggering the presumption against multiple punishments under Blockburger and Whalen. Under Missouri v. Hunter, the Double Jeopardy Clause permits cumulative punishments only if Congress clearly authorized them, but here Congress did not provide the kind of unmistakable cumulative-punishment directive it used elsewhere in § 924(c), and ambiguity should not be read to expand punishment. Interpreting the scheme to allow stacking would impose severe, duplicative penalties without a clear statement and would undermine procedural fairness by letting charging choices, rather than statutory clarity, drive sentencing exposure. Accordingly, one of the cumulative sentences must be vacated because Congress has not clearly authorized cumulation between § 924(c)(1)(A) and § 924(j) for the same conduct.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Congress authorized (and the Double Jeopardy Clause therefore permits) imposing cumulative punishments for a single firearm-related homicide by sentencing a defendant under both 18 U.S.C. § 924(j) and the lesser-included offense in 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)(1)(A) based on the same conduct/predicate crime.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. V (Double Jeopardy Clause); 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)(1)(A); 18 U.S.C. § 924(j).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Barrett argues that § 924(c)(1)(A) is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j) when both are predicated on the same underlying crime (here, Hobbs Act robbery) and the same firearm use, so the usual presumption against multiple punishments for the same offense applies. Because Congress did not clearly indicate an intent to allow stacking § 924(c) and § 924(j) punishments for the same conduct—and because § 924(c) expressly authorizes cumulative punishment in some contexts but does not do so for the § 924(c)/§ 924(j) pairing—the court should interpret the statutes to forbid cumulative sentences, vacate one conviction/sentence, and avoid a double-jeopardy problem.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Unusually, the United States supports Barrett: the government agrees § 924(c)(1)(A) is lesser-included within § 924(j) and that absent a clear statement from Congress authorizing cumulative punishments, courts should not impose both sentences for the same act. The government emphasizes that Congress knows how to expressly authorize cumulative punishments in § 924(c) but did not include any such authorization for cumulative sentencing between § 924(c)(1)(A) and § 924(j), so the presumption against cumulative punishments is not rebutted. (By contrast, the Court-appointed amicus defending the judgment below argues cumulative sentencing is permissible because § 924(j) should be understood as adding an additional offense/penalty layer on top of § 924(c) rather than displacing it, and contends precedent does not require both statutes to contain explicit cumulative-punishment language.)

John Roberts.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains that § 924(j) looks like a distinct offense with an added element (death), so Congress might have intended it to be separately punishable from § 924(c). But under Missouri v. Hunter, that inference is not enough; we need a clear textual authorization for cumulative punishment, and as Justice Kagan stresses, Congress repeatedly used explicit “in addition to” language elsewhere in § 924(c) but did not do so for the (c)/(j) pairing—making the silence meaningful. Blockburger therefore continues to function as the default rule of construction here because § 924(j) incorporates all elements of § 924(c) and adds only death, rendering (c) a lesser-included offense on the same facts. Justice Kavanaugh’s reliance on Lora strengthens a narrow, scheme-based resolution: § 924(j) supplies its own homicide-graded penalty tied to a (c) violation, and absent unmistakable direction we should not read it to mandate an additional consecutive § 924(c) sentence for the same conduct.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The strongest respondent argument—that § 924(c)’s “in addition to” and consecutive-sentencing directives reflect a general pro-stacking policy that should carry over to § 924(j)—fails because we apply that policy only where Congress clearly speaks to this pairing, not by inference. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, Blockburger is the default rule of construction for multiple punishments, and it is dispositive here because § 924(j) incorporates every element of § 924(c) and adds only death, making (c) a lesser-included offense on the same predicate and firearm use. Under Missouri v. Hunter, that presumption yields only to unmistakable textual authorization, and Justice Kagan’s point about Congress’s repeated, explicit cumulation language elsewhere in § 924(c) makes the silence regarding (c)/(j) meaningful. Lora, as Justice Kavanaugh notes, confirms § 924(j) has its own penalty provision, further undermining any claim that (c)’s mandatory consecutive term automatically stacks on top absent clear direction.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The strongest respondent argument—that § 924(j) is a distinct homicide offense with an added element (death) and thus should be separately punishable alongside § 924(c)—does not satisfy Missouri v. Hunter’s requirement of clear congressional authorization for cumulative punishments when one offense is lesser-included on the same facts. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress, Congress repeatedly used unmistakable “in addition to” and consecutive-sentencing language elsewhere in § 924(c), yet § 924(j) contains no comparable directive to stack an additional § 924(c) term on top of (j)’s own penalty provision. Justice Kavanaugh’s reliance on Lora reinforces the structural point: § 924(j) operates as a (c)-based homicide penalty scheme rather than silently importing (c)’s mandatory consecutive minimum as an extra layer for the same firearm use and predicate. Even accounting for practical consequences and law-enforcement interests, I cannot read punitive cumulation into statutory silence in a scheme where Congress knew precisely how to command it.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The strongest respondent-side contention would be that Congress intended § 924(j) as an additional homicide offense on top of § 924(c), so cumulative punishment is presumed; but under Missouri v. Hunter, that presumption cannot overcome Blockburger’s lesser-included-offense rule without a clear textual statement authorizing stacking. Justice Kagan’s point that Congress repeatedly used explicit “in addition to” language elsewhere in § 924(c) underscores that the silence here is meaningful, especially when § 924(j) simply incorporates (c)’s conduct plus death. Justice Gorsuch’s separation-of-powers and lenity concerns reinforce my pragmatic view that courts should not enlarge punishment through inference where the statutory scheme is at best ambiguous. Because § 924(c)(1)(A) is necessarily proved in a same-predicate § 924(j) prosecution, imposing both sentences risks precisely the kind of duplicative punishment the Double Jeopardy Clause’s multiple-punishments doctrine guards against absent unmistakable congressional authorization.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The strongest respondent point—that § 924(j) is separately codified, has its own penalty clause, and adds a death element—does not itself answer the multiple-punishments question, because Missouri v. Hunter requires clear congressional authorization to stack when one count is lesser-included on the same facts. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, Blockburger here is a tool for discerning that intent, and § 924(j)’s text “in the course of a violation of subsection (c)” makes (c) function as an incorporated base, not an extra add-on. Justice Kavanaugh’s reliance on Lora strengthens the structural inference: § 924(j) supplies its own penalty scheme keyed to (c), and Congress’s repeated use of explicit “in addition to” language elsewhere in § 924(c) makes the silence about stacking (c) and (j) meaningful rather than accidental. Given that contrast, any residual ambiguity should not be resolved to enlarge punishment by inference.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Respondent’s best point remains that § 924(j)’s separate subsection and penalty scheme suggests a distinct, cumulable offense, but as the Chief Justice notes, Missouri v. Hunter demands a clear textual authorization for cumulative punishment when § 924(c) is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j) on the same facts. Justice Kagan and Justice Kavanaugh persuasively emphasize the negative-implication evidence: Congress repeatedly used unmistakable “in addition to” and consecutive-sentence language elsewhere in § 924(c), yet omitted anything comparable for the (c)/(j) pairing, which is powerful textual proof against stacking. Lora (as Justice Kavanaugh highlights) underscores that § 924(j) supplies its own penalty scheme, making it especially implausible to assume it silently imports an extra mandatory § 924(c) term on top. With that statutory silence, separation-of-powers principles and lenity counsel against expanding punishment by inference, so one sentence must be vacated.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The strongest respondent point remains that § 924(j) is a distinct homicide offense with an added element (death), so Congress likely contemplated separate punishment; but under Missouri v. Hunter that inference cannot override Blockburger’s lesser-included-offense presumption absent a clear textual authorization to stack. Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s emphasis on Congress’s repeated use of explicit “in addition to” and consecutive-sentencing language elsewhere in § 924(c) makes the silence as to the (c)/(j) pairing especially telling in an institutionalist, text-and-structure analysis. Lora, as I noted and as Roberts echoes, reinforces that § 924(j) supplies its own penalty scheme keyed to a (c) violation, which undercuts any assumption that Congress silently required an additional mandatory consecutive § 924(c) term for the same conduct. Given that ambiguity and the serious multiple-punishments concern, I do not think we should expand sentencing exposure by implication.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The strongest respondent point—§ 924(j) is a separately codified homicide offense and thus presumptively stackable—does not supply the clear congressional authorization Missouri v. Hunter requires to impose cumulative punishment when Blockburger indicates a lesser-included offense. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Congress repeatedly used explicit “in addition to” and consecutive-sentencing language within § 924(c) when it wanted mandatory cumulation, and that textual contrast makes § 924(j)’s silence dispositive under a textualist approach. Justice Kavanaugh’s reliance on Lora further supports reading § 924(j) as having its own penalty scheme rather than silently importing an additional § 924(c) punishment on top for the same firearm use and predicate. Absent an unmistakable statement authorizing this particular stacking, we should not infer extra punishment from structure alone, so one sentence must be vacated.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The strongest respondent argument—that § 924(j) is a distinct offense with an added element (death) and thus can be cumulatively punished under Blockburger—does not carry the needed weight because Blockburger is only a proxy for congressional intent, and Missouri v. Hunter requires clear authorization for stacking when one count is a lesser-included offense on the same facts. As Justice Kagan emphasizes, Congress repeatedly used explicit “in addition to” language elsewhere in § 924(c), and that contrast makes the silence in § 924(j) especially telling rather than accidental. Justice Gorsuch’s separation-of-powers point reinforces my pragmatic concern: absent unmistakable direction, courts should not infer extra sentencing exposure that risks unfair double counting in a firearm-related homicide. Lora, as Justice Kavanaugh notes, supports reading § 924(j) as carrying its own penalty scheme tied to (c), not as silently importing an additional, consecutive (c) term on top for the very same conduct.

John Roberts.reasoning: The Double Jeopardy Clause permits cumulative punishments only when the legislature has clearly authorized them; otherwise the Blockburger/lesser-included-offense presumption against multiple punishments controls as a rule of statutory construction. Here, § 924(c)(1)(A) is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j) when both rest on the same predicate crime and the same firearm use, and nothing in § 924(j) or the surrounding scheme clearly states that Congress intended stacking these two punishments for the same conduct. Missouri v. Hunter teaches that clear legislative authorization can override the Blockburger presumption, but the absence of such a clear statement—especially given that § 924(c) elsewhere contains express cumulative-punishment directives—counsels a narrow ruling vacating the duplicative sentence to avoid a serious double-jeopardy question. That approach respects precedent and institutional legitimacy by deciding on statutory-intent grounds without expanding constitutional doctrine.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Double Jeopardy Clause bars cumulative punishments for the same offense unless Congress clearly authorized them. Applying Blockburger, § 924(c)(1)(A) is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j) when both rest on the same firearm use and predicate crime, triggering the presumption against multiple punishments. Under Missouri v. Hunter, that presumption yields only to a plainly expressed contrary legislative intent, and the text here supplies none: § 924(c) expressly mandates cumulation with certain other crimes but contains no clear statement authorizing stacking § 924(c)(1)(A) with § 924(j) for the same conduct. Reading the statutes according to their text and structure, Congress did not authorize two punishments for this single homicide, so one conviction/sentence must be vacated.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Double Jeopardy Clause permits cumulative punishments only if Congress clearly authorized them, and Blockburger functions here as a tool for discerning that intent. Because § 924(c)(1)(A) is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j) when both rest on the same predicate crime and the same firearm use, we should apply the presumption against multiple punishments absent a clear textual indication to the contrary. Nothing in § 924(j)’s text expressly authorizes stacking a § 924(c)(1)(A) sentence on top of the § 924(j) homicide punishment, and Congress’ demonstrated ability to mandate cumulative punishment elsewhere in § 924(c) underscores the absence of such an authorization here. Under Missouri v. Hunter, lacking that clear authorization, courts should not impose cumulative punishments for this single course of conduct.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Double Jeopardy Clause’s multiple-punishments protection turns on legislative intent: courts may not impose cumulative sentences for the same offense absent a clear congressional authorization. Here, § 924(c)(1)(A) is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j) when both rest on the same predicate crime and the same firearm use, triggering the ordinary presumption against multiple punishments under Blockburger’s rule of statutory construction and its progeny (e.g., Whalen and Garrett). Unlike the explicit cumulative-punishment directives Congress included elsewhere in § 924(c), nothing in § 924(j) clearly authorizes stacking a separate § 924(c) sentence on top of the § 924(j) homicide penalty for the same conduct, so the presumption is not rebutted. Under Missouri v. Hunter, that absence of a plainly expressed contrary intent means the court must avoid imposing greater punishment than Congress authorized and vacate one of the cumulative sentences.
